subtopic_detail: Prolonged episodes with closed eyes and side to side head movement captured on video telemetry with a normal trace
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to review a 24 year old woman on the neurology ward. She has been admitted for video electroencephalogram telemetry after two years of episodes in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive, and she has been taking levetiracetam without any change in frequency.

Three typical episodes have been captured. Each lasted around eight minutes with her eyes held closed, side to side head movement and asynchronous limb shaking that waxed and waned, and the trace showed a normal awake rhythm throughout with no post ictal slowing. The neurologist has explained the findings to her and she has asked to talk to someone about what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated with a euthymic affect, no focal neurological deficit, normal gait between episodes, no tongue biting and no incontinence during any recorded event, no injury from falls
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reported as normal, serum prolactin measured 20 minutes after a recorded episode within normal limits, electrolytes and glucose within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase the levetiracetam dose and add lamotrigine, reviewing her seizure diary again in the outpatient clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Escalating antiseizure medication treats a condition that the telemetry has excluded and exposes her to adverse effects including irritability and rash for no benefit. Escalation would be correct if the recorded events had shown an ictal electrographic correlate. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder

options.text: Tell her the episodes are not genuine seizures, discharge her from the service and ask her general practitioner to arrange counselling
options.rationale: Framing the diagnosis as an absence of real illness is the single commonest reason these patients disengage, and it is both inaccurate and therapeutically destructive. The explanation must convey a positive diagnosis of a recognised disorder with an evidence based treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis using the telemetry findings and refer her for psychological therapy while planning antiseizure drug withdrawal
options.rationale: Delivering the diagnosis well, showing the patient the recorded events and the normal trace, and referring for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted to functional seizures is the treatment with the best evidence, and withdrawing an ineffective antiseizure drug is part of that plan. A substantial proportion of patients improve on the explanation alone. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as the primary treatment for the episodes and arrange psychiatric review in three months
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a role where there is comorbid depression or anxiety but they are not a primary treatment for functional seizures, in which psychological therapy has the stronger evidence. Medication as monotherapy here would leave the central treatment undelivered. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder

options.text: Repeat the magnetic resonance imaging with an epilepsy protocol and arrange a further period of inpatient telemetry in three months time
options.rationale: Repeating investigations that have already given a clear positive answer reinforces the belief that something has been missed and delays treatment. Further imaging would be justified only if new focal signs or a new event semiology appeared. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder

explanation.summary: Functional seizures, also called psychogenic non epileptic seizures or dissociative seizures, account for around a fifth of patients referred to specialist epilepsy services and a similar proportion of apparent status epilepticus presentations. Video electroencephalogram telemetry capturing a typical event with a normal trace is the reference standard, and supportive semiological features include eye closure during the event, side to side head movement, asynchronous and waxing and waning limb movements, prolonged duration, absence of tongue biting or incontinence, and a normal post event prolactin. The diagnosis is positive rather than one of exclusion, and how it is communicated strongly predicts outcome, so the explanation should name the condition, affirm that the episodes are involuntary and real, use the recorded evidence, and immediately offer treatment. Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for functional seizures is the intervention with the strongest randomised evidence. Around one in ten patients also has epilepsy, so antiseizure medication is withdrawn thoughtfully rather than abruptly stopped.
key_points: Video telemetry capturing a typical event with a normal trace is the reference standard.
Eye closure, asynchronous waxing and waning movements and prolonged duration support the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is positive and must be communicated as a real, involuntary and treatable condition.
Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for functional seizures has the strongest evidence.
Around ten per cent of patients have coexisting epilepsy, so drug withdrawal is planned carefully.
explanation.pearls: Serum prolactin rises to at least twice baseline within 10 to 20 minutes of a generalised tonic clonic seizure and returns to normal by an hour, so a normal level taken in that window supports a functional event, but a normal level is meaningless if the sample is taken later or if the event was focal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Non epileptic seizures

subtopic_detail: Sudden uncontrollable crying spells months after a stroke in a man whose sleep, appetite and interests are unchanged
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 68 year old man in a stroke follow up clinic four months after a right hemisphere infarct. His wife reports that he bursts into tears several times a day, often triggered by something trivial like a television advertisement, and that the crying stops as abruptly as it starts.

He is embarrassed by it and says he does not feel sad when it happens. He has returned to lawn bowls twice a week and enjoys it, sleeps through the night and eats normally. His wife says his weight has been steady and he has not spoken about wanting to die.

data_table.Examination: Mild residual left sided weakness with independent mobility, speech fluent, euthymic affect between episodes with reactive expression, no psychomotor retardation, mini mental state examination 28 out of 30, no anhedonia elicited on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and explain that it reduces the frequency of the episodes
options.rationale: Preserved mood, sleep, appetite and enjoyment alongside abrupt stereotyped crying that does not match the inner emotional state identifies pseudobulbar affect, which responds to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at doses lower and with a latency shorter than those needed for depression. Explaining the mechanism to the couple relieves much of the embarrassment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Commence a full antidepressant dose for post stroke depression and review his mood using a structured rating scale in six weeks
options.rationale: Post stroke depression is the near pair worth excluding, but it causes sustained low mood with anhedonia and disturbance of sleep and appetite, and this man retains enjoyment of bowls and sleeps and eats normally. Full antidepressant dosing would be the right approach if those features were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Commence a low dose atypical antipsychotic to reduce the emotional lability and review his response in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics carry a raised risk of stroke and death in older people with cerebrovascular disease and have no evidence base in this condition. They are reserved for psychosis or for severe behavioural disturbance in dementia where other measures have failed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the depressive cognitions underlying his frequent episodes of crying
options.rationale: There are no depressive cognitions to target, since he does not feel sad during the episodes and his mood is otherwise normal. Psychological therapy is valuable for genuine post stroke depression and for adjustment difficulties after stroke. (Source: RANZCP: Depression in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Depression in older people

options.text: Reassure his wife that the crying is a normal grief reaction to his stroke and review him again in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: Adjustment distress after stroke produces sadness that is congruent with the situation and builds and fades gradually, rather than abrupt stereotyped episodes triggered by trivial stimuli. Leaving a treatable and socially disabling symptom untreated for three months is not justified when an effective option exists. (Source: RANZCP: Depression in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Depression in older people

explanation.summary: Pseudobulbar affect describes involuntary, stereotyped outbursts of crying or laughing that are disproportionate to, or incongruent with, the person's inner emotional state, and it arises when lesions disconnect cortical and cerebellar inhibition of brainstem centres for emotional expression. It complicates stroke, motor neurone disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury and dementia, and is commonly mislabelled as depression because relatives describe frequent crying. The distinguishing features are the abruptness and stereotypy of the episodes, their trivial or absent triggers, the mismatch between the display and the felt emotion, and the preservation of sleep, appetite, interest and mood between episodes. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclics both reduce episode frequency, typically at lower doses and with a faster onset than in depression, which supports a distinct mechanism. Recognition matters because the symptom is profoundly socially isolating and patients often withdraw from public activities out of embarrassment.
key_points: Episodes are abrupt, stereotyped and incongruent with the person's inner emotional state.
Sleep, appetite, interest and between episode mood are preserved, unlike in depression.
The mechanism is disconnection of cortical inhibition of brainstem emotional expression.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors work at lower doses and faster than in depression.
The symptom is socially disabling and frequently misattributed to post stroke depression.
explanation.pearls: Expect a response to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor in pseudobulbar affect within one to two weeks rather than the four to six weeks required for depression, so a lack of any change by three weeks should prompt a review of the diagnosis rather than simply waiting longer.

subtopic_detail: Four days of reduced sleep need with overspending and pressured speech six weeks into treatment for a depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32 year old man who was started on sertraline six weeks ago by his general practitioner for a moderate depressive episode. His partner brought him in today because for the past four days he has been sleeping about three hours a night and waking full of energy.

He has spent 14000 dollars on recording equipment he does not need, is talking so fast that his partner cannot interrupt, and has emailed his manager a plan to restructure the company. He says he has never felt better. His mother was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in her thirties for something his family never discussed.

data_table.Examination: Elevated and expansive mood with pressured speech and flight of ideas, grandiose but not delusional content, no hallucinations, insight absent, orientated with intact attention, no tremor, no clonus and no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline at the current dose and add a short course of a hypnotic to restore his sleep while his mood is monitored
options.rationale: Continuing the antidepressant leaves the likely driver of the switch in place, and treating only the insomnia addresses a symptom while the manic episode escalates. Hypnotics may be used as an adjunct, but never in place of ceasing the precipitant and starting antimanic treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose, arrange review in two weeks and advise his partner to bring him back sooner if his behaviour worsens
options.rationale: A partial dose reduction with a two week interval underestimates both the speed at which mania escalates and the financial and occupational harm already occurring. Dose reduction with close review is a reasonable approach to mild hypomanic symptoms in a patient with insight and a supportive environment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add lithium to the sertraline as an augmentation strategy and arrange measurement of his serum level in one week
options.rationale: Lithium is an effective antimanic agent but works too slowly for an acute episode used alone, and adding it while continuing the antidepressant leaves the precipitant in place. Augmenting an antidepressant with lithium is a strategy for treatment resistant unipolar depression, not for an emergent manic episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Cease the sertraline and commence an atypical antipsychotic with antimanic efficacy, arranging urgent specialist psychiatric review
options.rationale: Antidepressant emergent mania is managed by stopping the antidepressant and starting an agent with established antimanic efficacy such as olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, with urgent review because insight is absent and the financial and occupational risk is active. The family history and the switch itself both point to an underlying bipolar diathesis that changes long term management. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Switch him from sertraline to a different class of antidepressant such as mirtazapine and review his sleep and mood in two weeks
options.rationale: Every antidepressant class can precipitate a switch in a person with bipolar diathesis, so exchanging one for another perpetuates the risk rather than removing it. Switching antidepressant class is a strategy for inadequate response or intolerable adverse effects in unipolar depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Antidepressant emergent mania is one of the clearest signals that an apparently unipolar depressive episode is part of a bipolar illness, and it typically appears within the first weeks to months of starting treatment. Risk factors include a family history of bipolar disorder, early onset depression, psychotic features, a rapid response to antidepressants and previous subthreshold hypomanic periods, and a careful collateral history often uncovers these before the switch occurs. Management requires ceasing the antidepressant and treating the manic episode in its own right with an antipsychotic with antimanic efficacy, lithium or valproate, with the choice shaped by the acuity, the patient's sex and reproductive plans, and any previous response. Reduced need for sleep rather than simple insomnia is the most discriminating single symptom of mania, because the person wakes energised rather than tired. Long term, the diagnosis shifts towards bipolar disorder, mood stabilisation becomes the foundation of treatment and future antidepressant use requires mood stabiliser cover.
key_points: A switch to mania on an antidepressant is a strong marker of underlying bipolar disorder.
Reduced need for sleep with preserved energy discriminates mania from simple insomnia.
Cease the antidepressant rather than reducing it or switching class.
Treat the episode with an agent of established antimanic efficacy and arrange urgent review.
Absent insight with active financial or occupational harm raises the urgency of assessment.
explanation.pearls: Valproate must not be used as the antimanic agent in any person who could become pregnant unless the conditions of a pregnancy prevention programme are met, because first trimester exposure carries a roughly 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a 30 to 40 per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Severe pain from a fractured tibia in a man maintained on sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid dependence
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar providing addiction medicine liaison to the orthopaedic ward. A 34 year old man was admitted overnight with a tibial shaft fracture after falling from a ladder and is awaiting internal fixation this afternoon.

He takes sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone 16 mg daily, dispensed daily at his community pharmacy, and has been abstinent from other opioids for two years. He rates his pain 9 out of 10 despite regular paracetamol, and the orthopaedic intern has telephoned you because he is reluctant to prescribe opioids to a patient on an opioid treatment programme.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain with the right leg in a backslab, no sedation with a normal level of alertness, pupils mid position, no withdrawal signs, no track marks, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for buprenorphine only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his analgesia?

options.text: Withhold all opioid analgesia and manage his pain with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory and a regional nerve block alone
options.rationale: Denying opioids to a patient with a fractured tibia because of a history of dependence is a well described inequity that leaves severe acute pain untreated and destabilises recovery. Non opioid and regional techniques are valuable adjuncts but will not cover the pain of a tibial shaft fracture on their own. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Cease the buprenorphine immediately and transfer him to methadone so that full agonist analgesia can work without receptor competition
options.rationale: Switching maintenance agents during an acute admission is destabilising, takes days to achieve and is unnecessary because effective analgesia is achievable alongside continued buprenorphine. A planned transfer is a decision for his community prescriber in the outpatient setting. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Halve his buprenorphine dose today so that receptor occupancy falls and any full agonist opioid given afterwards becomes more effective
options.rationale: Reducing the maintenance dose risks precipitating withdrawal, which worsens pain perception, and the analgesic benefit does not offset that harm. Dose reduction is considered only in complex cases in discussion with an addiction medicine specialist and a pain service. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Continue his usual buprenorphine dose and add titrated short acting full agonist opioid analgesia with multimodal and regional adjuncts
options.rationale: Continuing maintenance buprenorphine and adding a titrated full agonist alongside paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory and regional techniques is the Australian standard, and higher than usual full agonist doses are often required because buprenorphine occupies a high proportion of receptors. Stopping the maintenance dose is what causes problems, not continuing it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Prescribe regular tramadol as the sole opioid agent because its partial mechanism is considered safer in a person with opioid dependence
options.rationale: Tramadol is a weak opioid with an unreliable analgesic effect that depends on cytochrome P450 2D6 metabolism, and it adds a seizure and serotonin toxicity risk without providing adequate analgesia for a long bone fracture. Choosing it out of caution provides the appearance of treatment rather than treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Patients maintained on buprenorphine frequently receive inadequate analgesia after injury or surgery because clinicians fear precipitating relapse, causing respiratory depression or interfering with the treatment programme, and each of those fears is largely unfounded. Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial agonist that occupies a large fraction of mu receptors at therapeutic doses, so full agonists still work but often require higher doses and closer titration, and the safest course is to continue the maintenance dose rather than to withhold or reduce it. Multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, a non steroidal anti-inflammatory where not contraindicated, regional blockade and ketamine reduces the full agonist requirement substantially. Untreated acute pain is itself a potent trigger for relapse, so effective analgesia is part of addiction treatment rather than a threat to it. The community prescriber and the dispensing pharmacy must be contacted so that the maintenance dose continues accurately and the discharge plan is coordinated.
key_points: Continue the usual maintenance buprenorphine dose through the acute admission.
Full agonist opioids remain effective but often require higher doses and closer titration.
Multimodal and regional techniques substantially reduce the full agonist requirement.
Untreated acute pain is itself a major trigger for relapse.
Contact the community prescriber and pharmacy to coordinate dosing and discharge.
explanation.pearls: Naloxone in the sublingual combination product has negligible bioavailability by that route and exists only to deter injection, so it neither blocks the buprenorphine nor blocks the added full agonist and is not a reason to withhold analgesia.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

subtopic_detail: Private disclosure of a son withdrawing money without permission by a woman with intact cognition who asks for secrecy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an aged care assessment clinic seeing an 82 year old woman referred for low mood. Her son has driven her in and answered most of your questions until you asked to see her on her own.

Alone with you she becomes tearful and says her son has been taking money from her account without asking, that he shouts at her when she questions it, and that she is frightened of him becoming angry. She has not been hurt and is not afraid to go home today. She then asks you not to tell anyone because she does not want to lose contact with her grandchildren.

data_table.Examination: Mild reactive low mood with no psychotic features and no suicidal ideation, Montreal cognitive assessment 27 out of 30, able to describe her financial situation and to weigh the options you discuss and communicate a consistent choice, no bruising or injury on examination, well nourished and well kempt
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Telephone the police today to report the financial abuse, explaining to her afterwards that you were obliged to make the report
options.rationale: Acting against the expressed wishes of an adult with decision making capacity removes her control at the very moment she has entrusted you with the disclosure, and it frequently ends the therapeutic relationship and her access to help. Police involvement without consent is justified where there is an immediate risk of serious harm or where capacity is impaired. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Raise the allegation with her son at the end of the consultation so that he can give his account before any further action is taken
options.rationale: Confronting the alleged perpetrator without her consent breaches confidentiality and can directly escalate the risk to her when they leave together. Any conversation with family occurs only with her agreement and after a safety plan is in place. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Document the disclosure, assess her safety and her capacity, and with her consent connect her to elder abuse advocacy with planned review
options.rationale: She has intact capacity, is not in immediate danger, and is entitled to decide what happens next, so the task is careful documentation, an explicit safety assessment, information about the national elder abuse helpline and advocacy services, and a follow up appointment that keeps the door open. Most older people disclose gradually, and maintaining the relationship is what eventually enables action. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Apply to the civil and administrative tribunal for a financial management order so that her money is protected from further withdrawals
options.rationale: A financial management order removes a person's legal right to manage her own affairs and is available only where capacity to make financial decisions is impaired, which is not the case here. Her capacity is intact and the appropriate protective instrument is her own decision making, supported by advice. (Source: Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report)
source_refs: Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report

options.text: Accept her request for confidentiality, treat the low mood with an antidepressant and take no further action regarding the disclosure
options.rationale: Respecting her wishes does not mean doing nothing, because documentation, safety assessment and offering information all sit within her consent and are what make later action possible. Treating the mood symptom alone medicalises a situation whose cause is the abuse itself. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

explanation.summary: Elder abuse affects around one in six older Australians living in the community, with financial and psychological abuse the commonest forms and adult children the commonest perpetrators. Disclosure is often partial and hedged with requests for secrecy, driven by shame, fear of losing contact with family and fear of being moved into residential care, and how the clinician responds to that first disclosure largely determines whether the person ever discloses again. The governing principle is that an adult with decision making capacity has the right to make choices that others consider unwise, so the clinician's role is to assess capacity and immediate safety, document carefully and contemporaneously, offer information and referral, and arrange review. Seeing the person alone is essential and should be routine rather than exceptional, since a controlling relative who answers all questions is itself a warning sign. Overriding the person's wishes is reserved for impaired capacity or a serious and immediate risk of harm, and mandatory reporting obligations differ between jurisdictions and in residential aged care.
key_points: Financial abuse by an adult child is the commonest pattern of elder abuse in Australia.
Always interview the older person alone, particularly when a relative answers for them.
An adult with capacity has the right to decline intervention, including reporting.
Document contemporaneously, assess safety and capacity, and offer advocacy and helpline contacts.
Override the person's wishes only for impaired capacity or immediate serious risk.
explanation.pearls: An enduring power of attorney executed while the person had capacity does not entitle the attorney to use the money for their own benefit, and a relative who describes withdrawals as an early inheritance is describing a breach of fiduciary duty that the state tribunal can review and reverse.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse
Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report

subtopic_detail: Foster child who does not seek comfort from carers but plays reciprocally with peers and uses imaginative play
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent service seeing a six year old boy who has lived with the same foster carers since he was three, following removal for severe neglect. His carer reports that when he falls over or is frightened he does not come to her, and that he accepts comfort from her stiffly when she offers it.

She says he seems flat and rarely shows pleasure at home, and she feels she has never got close to him. His teacher describes him as quiet but says he plays chasing and building games with two particular friends, takes turns, and spent most of last week running an elaborate pretend restaurant in the classroom corner.

data_table.Examination: Reserved with restricted positive affect during the interview, good eye contact and appropriate social reciprocity with the interviewer, spontaneous imaginative play with the toys offered, no restricted or repetitive interests, no sensory sensitivities reported, speech and language age appropriate, no overfamiliarity with strangers
data_table.Investigations: Hearing screen normal, growth parameters on the 25th centile, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him for an autism spectrum assessment as the first step, since reduced emotional reciprocity with carers is the central concern
options.rationale: Autism is the differential that matters most here, but it is argued against by his reciprocal peer play, spontaneous imaginative play, age appropriate language and absence of restricted interests or sensory differences. Assessment would be the priority if the social difficulty extended across all relationships rather than being confined to attachment figures. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children

options.text: Refer the child and his carer together for an attachment focused dyadic intervention and provide ongoing support to the foster placement
options.rationale: Persistent failure to seek or respond to comfort with limited positive affect in a child with a history of neglect, in the presence of normal peer social functioning, is reactive attachment disorder, and the treatment is a dyadic intervention that works with the child and carer together while supporting placement stability. No medication treats the disorder itself. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children

options.text: Commence a low dose of risperidone to address his emotional flatness and his difficulty in forming a relationship with his foster carer
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no role in attachment disorders and carry metabolic and extrapyramidal risks that are particularly undesirable in a young child. Their use in this age group is limited to severe aggression or irritability in specific neurodevelopmental contexts after psychosocial measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer him for individual play therapy without carer involvement so that he can build a therapeutic relationship free of family dynamics
options.rationale: The disorder resides in the relationship rather than in the child alone, so an intervention that deliberately excludes the carer cannot address it and forgoes the mechanism of change. Individual therapy has a place for specific trauma symptoms alongside, not instead of, dyadic work. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for his flat affect and reduced enjoyment and review his progress again in six weeks
options.rationale: The restricted positive affect here is a feature of the attachment disorder rather than a depressive episode, and there is no pervasive low mood, sleep or appetite disturbance to support antidepressant treatment. An antidepressant would be considered if a clear comorbid depressive disorder emerged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Reactive attachment disorder arises when a young child experiences grossly insufficient care, such as severe neglect or repeated changes of primary caregiver, before the capacity for selective attachment has formed. The child shows a consistent pattern of not seeking and not responding to comfort from caregivers, together with limited positive affect and episodes of unexplained irritability, sadness or fearfulness even during non threatening interactions with the carer. It must be distinguished from autism spectrum disorder, where the social communication difficulty is pervasive across all relationships and is accompanied by restricted interests, repetitive behaviours and often language difference, none of which fit a child who plays imaginatively and reciprocally with peers. Its counterpart, disinhibited social engagement disorder, produces the opposite presentation of overfamiliarity with unfamiliar adults and persists even after placement improves. Treatment is psychosocial and focuses on the caregiving relationship, and placement stability is the strongest determinant of outcome, so supporting the foster carer is a therapeutic act in itself.
key_points: Reactive attachment disorder requires a history of grossly insufficient early care.
The child fails to seek or respond to comfort and shows limited positive affect with carers.
Normal reciprocal peer play and imaginative play argue strongly against autism.
Treatment is dyadic and psychosocial, and no medication treats the disorder itself.
Placement stability is the strongest single determinant of long term outcome.
explanation.pearls: Disinhibited social engagement disorder is the one attachment presentation that persists after the caregiving environment improves, so a child who continues to wander off with unfamiliar adults years into a stable placement needs ongoing supervision planning rather than reassurance that the placement has fixed the problem.

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of aggression, fire setting and cruelty to a pet in a boy who concentrates well in class
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a nine year old boy referred after he was suspended for the third time this year. Over the past eighteen months he has started fires in the garden shed twice, has repeatedly hit smaller children, and his mother found the family cat with its whiskers cut off.

He tells you flatly that he does not care whether the other children were hurt. His teacher reports that he sits still, sustains attention through a forty minute lesson and completes his written work, and that the aggression is planned rather than impulsive. His mother is exhausted and says she has given up trying to set rules.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative with a restricted range of affect, no remorse expressed when discussing the incidents, no psychotic symptoms, no depressive symptoms elicited, intelligence appears within the normal range with age appropriate reading, no injuries or signs of maltreatment
data_table.Investigations: Teacher and parent behaviour rating scales showing elevated conduct scores with attention and hyperactivity scores within the normal range, hearing and vision screening normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence methylphenidate and titrate the dose over four weeks, reviewing his teacher's behaviour ratings at each dose increase
options.rationale: Stimulant treatment is effective for aggression that is driven by impulsivity in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, but his attention ratings are normal, he sustains attention through a full lesson and the aggression is planned rather than impulsive. Treating conduct problems with stimulants in the absence of the disorder does not work. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone to reduce his aggression while the family waits for a place in a longer term treatment programme
options.rationale: Risperidone reduces aggression modestly but at the cost of substantial weight gain, metabolic disturbance and hyperprolactinaemia in a growing child, and it does not address the parenting and family factors that maintain the behaviour. It is reserved for severe aggression that persists despite an adequate trial of psychosocial treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer his mother to a structured parent management training programme and coordinate a consistent behaviour plan with his school
options.rationale: Structured parent management training combined with school liaison has the strongest evidence of any intervention for conduct disorder in this age group and directly addresses the collapse of consistent limit setting that his mother describes. It remains first line even when callous and unemotional traits are present, although the response is somewhat smaller. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him for individual anger management counselling and review his behaviour in the clinic again after twelve weekly sessions
options.rationale: Individual work with the child alone has a markedly weaker evidence base than family based treatment at this age, and anger management specifically targets impulsive rage rather than the planned instrumental aggression described here. Individual cognitive work has more to offer adolescents than primary school aged children. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Make a notification to the statutory child protection agency on the basis that cruelty to animals indicates that he is being maltreated
options.rationale: Cruelty to animals is a symptom of conduct disorder as well as a possible marker of maltreatment, and there are no injuries, no disclosure and no other indicators of harm in this assessment. A notification is required where there is a reasonable belief that the child is at risk of significant harm. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour that violates the basic rights of others or major age appropriate social norms, spanning aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. Distinguishing it from attention deficit hyperactivity disorder matters because the two frequently coexist and because aggression that is impulsive and driven by inattention responds to stimulants, whereas planned instrumental aggression in a child with normal attention does not. The specifier of limited prosocial emotions, sometimes described as callous and unemotional traits, identifies a subgroup with lack of remorse, shallow affect and indifference to performance, who have a worse trajectory and a somewhat reduced response to standard treatment but who still improve with it. Parent management training remains first line across the age range, with multisystemic therapy and functional family therapy used for adolescents with more entrenched difficulties. Medication is adjunctive and targets comorbidity or severe residual aggression rather than the disorder itself.
key_points: Planned instrumental aggression with normal attention ratings argues against attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Parent management training with school liaison is first line and has the strongest evidence.
Limited prosocial emotions predict a worse trajectory but do not change the first line treatment.
Antipsychotics are adjunctive and reserved for severe aggression after psychosocial treatment fails.
Always screen for maltreatment, learning difficulty and substance use as maintaining factors.
explanation.pearls: Screen explicitly for a specific learning disorder in every child presenting with conduct problems, because undetected reading difficulty is present in around a third and the daily experience of failing in class is a powerful maintaining factor that no parenting programme can undo on its own.
